A lot of the advice on here is situational depending on the game and group you're playing with. You know the people at your table better than we do, try to make an educated guess as to what you'll be doing more of, fighting or roleplaying. Being the only roleplayer in a kick-the-door-down game gets old, and vice versa.

Ultimately D&D is about telling an awesome tale together, all the numbers and rules in the world just help us shape that story. When you make your character, don't think about what makes him the best fighter or the best wizard - think about what makes him an interesting story you'd want to hear get told to the end.

When making a character, I try to answer three basic questions about them:

  • Why are they out adventuring?

Going out and raiding dungeons or fighting gnolls is dangerous, and not something done by most folks. Why is your character doing it? A cheap answer like "he needs money" will get you a cheap character, try looking beyond and giving the DM something like "he needs money to buy supplies so his cabin up in the mountains has enough food to last the winter" or "he's trying to put together a team to break his best friend out of prison."

  • What will they do once they're done adventuring?

There are some characters that plan on adventuring until they drop dead, but even the most battle-hungry warriors know that they'll eventually get old and need to settle down a bit. Does he want to return to his homeland after proving his innocence? Does he want to be the captain of the guard at the fort where he grew up? Maybe he wants to build a workshop so he can finally research his spells in peace!

  • What's the biggest challenge they're working through?

This usually works out best if you make it a story or personality challenge instead of a physical one. Maybe all the other nobles essentially blackmailed him out of his family estate? Maybe everyone in town thinks he's cursed? Maybe he's still bitter about finding out his childhood hero is actually an arrogant bastard? Maybe he's trying to reform a corrupt church?

My advice is you shouldn't be asking the internet this question. You should be asking your DM and fellow players this question. Really. Every answer here had better be predicated with something along the lines of "consider the style of play your group has and then..." Assuming the people you're playing with are experienced, especially your DM, they're all going to have a lot of actually valuable/applicable advice to give you.

Hmmm. In that case, I would do the following:

  1. Don't worry about doing anything other than having fun because, without at least one somewhat experienced player in the group, what you'll be playing will be... D&Dish at best.
  2. Roll up a bunch, and I mean a bunch, of 1st level puds. Give them all a spin. Experience just how fragile a 1st level character is. Feel how great it is to make it to 2nd level.
  3. If you find yourself not liking the game, I would totally understand. That said, I would urge you to hold your final opinion until you've played with at least two experienced DM's. In my opinion, the DM makes or breaks the game. Think of learning to play D&D (or, I would argue, role-playing games in general) as kinda like learning kung fu. Sure, you can teach yourself... ish. But the amazing reality is just about every martial artist out there can trace their lineage back to a just a handful of original masters. They all learned from someone more experienced who came before them. So too with D&D players.
  4. Rather than thinking of D&D as a game, I like to think of it as a hobby. The more time and effort you invest in it, the more fun you'lll have. I've been playing since 1979, and my only regret is there are just too few hours in the day to spend as much time on it as I would like.
  5. Regarding min/max'ing. sigh Might as well argue religion. It's fair to say I'm not interested in that style of play, but I also recognize the merits in doing so. You'll have to discover for yourself what kind of player you are. I will say, however, that min/max-ers and non min/max-ers in the same group are not gonna mix well.

And finally...

This is gonna sound strange, but while the DM may be the "boss" of the game, it is not her story. The story belongs to everyone at the table. The success of the game rests on everyones shoulders. The DM is not directing a bunch of player actors. Instead, I like to think of the DM as an instigator and the players are her accomplices.

I really hope your group has a blast!

Story telling 101. We read about how a protagonist is placed in danger, adapts and overcomes to triumph.

Use the same principle for your character. He/She is at the beginning of a huge adventure. What was their normal life like before they were pushed to become an adventurer? Were they bored? Trapped to family obligations? Indebted to a village elder?

What moral/psychological flaws do they have? Do they ALWAYS have to save the innocent. Do they only care about their own race? Are you afraid of certain elements? Hate magic users? Patronising and small minded?

I don't play what most would consider conventional tabletop games, but I've got enough experience with RPGs in various formats to say that you should ask the GM about what precisely they have in mind for the game. Some GMs like to have what amount to hack-fests where there's blood and gore and player characters die in droves with little intellectual interaction or conversation. Others like to have deeply intellectual situations that have very little combat. Most are in between. You can tailor your character to what's best here. Furthermore, ask the GM if there are any "house rules," as most games have at least some rules they go with that are unique. It has often been said that "Rule 0" of any RPG system is "the Game Master can override whatever they see fit," and that's pretty accurate.

Gary Gygax, the creator of D&D, was brilliant in many ways, but I particularly liked how he combined things, like a master chef, almost. For example, instead of having something like a standard Ettin monster, with two heads, he would have a one headed Ettin, who would be having a terrible time for some reason, due to not having his other head, which might have been lost in battle. This could lead to a mini-story. Try and find stories everywhere. They bring the world to life!

Use your imagination! If your Party encounters, for example, a NonPlayerCharacter group with some treasure, instead of immediately working out the best way to kill them and take their treasure, use your imagination. Maybe you could try paying them to act as your henchmen. Maybe you could try and help them! Maybe you could try and get them to change their fashion or something funny.

Have a good game!
